title: Intelligence is not the main bottleneck
excerpt: Confessions of a naive hamster: why the smartest people in the room keep missing that intelligence is often not the main bottleneck in the real world
content_html:
Edit: To be clear, I'm not saying everyone or even a majority of people in the SF tech scene think this way. But some certainly do (e.g. the opening conversation is verbatim) and this post is about a particular core scene whose views carry disproportionate weight in the discourse and in policymaking.

At a recent dinner, someone from an AI lab asked me, quite bluntly , why I do what I do — why I write about the regulatory bottlenecks to medical progress, why I spend my time on policies related to clinical trials. He looked at me with something best summarized as pity.

I told him what I believe: that in the age of AI, medicine will be bottlenecked more than ever by regulation and the grind of clinical trials, and that billions poured into faster pre-clinical research won’t touch that problem, unsexy as it is. I brought up housing: we’ve had the technology to build better housing for decades, yet it’s more expensive than ever, because housing is a question of political will, not pure capability.

He looked at me incredulously. Surely, a smart person like me should know that AI, or better said, AGI will be hyperpersuasive soon – already on a bunch of benchmarks it exceeds professional debaters at persuasion. I said, “Hmm.” He said, “Yes, yes”, with the undertone of a man who knows things deeply, things that mere mortals like me, not being AI lab employees, are simply not well placed to grasp. And he looked at me again with that sense of pity, the way one looks at a slightly mentally impaired but cute animal awaiting its imminent slaughter.

That night I lay awake, twisting and turning, wondering whether my life had any point at all. Whether every decision I’d ever made had been, in some way, a mistake. What could I have done better?

But as the sun came up, I found my way back to the same thought: no matter how “intelligent” AI becomes, intelligence is often not the main bottleneck to things changing in the real world. It is hard to hold on to that conviction when people smarter than you, with access to privileged information, insist otherwise. After all, this could all just be “cope” from the naive hamster awaiting its slaughter.

But, I shall nonetheless stick to my beliefs.

Because the people at these labs made fortunes betting on ideas that once looked insane, the world now takes nearly everything they say on faith. That, I think, is a mistake. It is not a given that AI will solve the problems most people actually care about, including medicine, unless we think about those problems clearly. And at the moment, I don’t believe we are or at least, not to the extent that we could. My case is simple, and it comes from two directions. One is what I observe in the social dynamics of San Francisco, and in how people there talk about all this. The other is what I notice in a field I happen to know something about: medicine.

One of the promises most often invoked to justify AI’s risks is that it will “cure disease.” Every major AI lab CEO says it, and investors seems to agree: any biotech startup with an AI story attached commands an impressive valuation, even as more conventional biotechs struggle for funding and die. But this whole enterprise, as I have long argued, is bottlenecked by many things that have little to do with “intelligence” as such, and the degree to which that often goes unacknowledged is strange to watch.

The evidence is everywhere, if you treat scientific advancement as a rough proxy for intelligence and ask whether it alone unblocks progress. Take Eroom’s Law: the number of new drugs approved per dollar of R&D has fallen for decades, even as our scientific tools have grown vastly more powerful, the exact opposite of what the existence of more raw capability would predict. Or take a company like Adaptimmune, which has brought two transformative therapies to market in rare cancers and is nonetheless fighting to stay alive, due to the cost of developing them. Or one can listen to the scientists behind “baby KJ,” the infant saved by a bespoke gene-editing therapy: they have everything they need scientifically and still cannot easily repeat it for the next child, because manufacturing costs, driven in part by regulatory requirements, stand in the way.

In biopharma specifically, one great bottleneck is clinical trials (I know I keep banging on about this), which today consume something like seven years and cost more than a billion dollars per drug. And trials are not a mere formality. They generate precisely the kind of data that would train better models in the first place: human data, which is ultimately irreplaceable.

We have extensive evidence faster clinical trials are important for biomedical innovation, both directly and indirectly, through second-order effects (like increasing the risk appetite of those working in the industry and helping better align incentive through fast feedback loops). This ranges from robust economic papers showing shorter trials massively boost investment in a disease area, all else equal, to the natural experiment of China. China is threatening to race ahead of US in biotech, with Chinese biotechs encompassing more than a half of big Western pharma licensing deals. A mere decade ago, this percentage was zero. This transformation happened while China remains worse in terms of basic science, mostly due to regulatory reforms that allow faster iterative learning using in-human data1.

Trials themselves can be made shorter, more informative and better, including with AI. One area I am particularly bullish on is surrogate endpoints and biomarkers, where AI could turn discrete, coarse readouts of whether a drug is working into fast, continuous ones. This would in turn optimize trials immensely. For some indications, the gain could be as high as 10x faster and cheaper trials if the right surrogates are found. And this is not even considering the benefits of simply optimizing the trials without necessarily shortening them: imagine having the right biomarker that tells you whether a therapy is working early enough.

But even here the binding constraint is not entirely intelligence. Quite often, it is governance. I keep talking to companies trying to build exactly these biomarkers, and what they run into, again and again, is how hard it is to access the underlying data. Some have been waiting for a year for the NIH to release imaging datasets they can use to produce better biomarkers. If one needs to interact with the FDA to get their endpoint validated, it is even worse: I have previously written about how the validation of Bone Mineral Density (BMD) for use as a surrogate endpoint in osteoporosis trials took 12 years (!), despite the fact that the data to support it already existed in full and the analyses done were basically regressions.

When people in the AI sphere do engage with regulation and governance in medicine, it often seems to happen in a rather superficial way. I have seen many times that argument that because most drugs fail for lack of efficacy, regulation can’t explain much of the slow-down in medical progress compared to basic science that we have witnessed in the last decades: after all, approving more inefficacious drugs won’t help. This analysis sounds superficially true, but it’s not. As I keep saying, when people talk about the importance of regulation in slowing down biomedical progress, they rarely mean the approval decision at the end. It is about the entire process upstream: how easily human data can be collected, and then how easily, once collected, it can actually be used.

I know most about clinical trials, but this is not the only area where governance and policy slows down progress. Another example is related to how the structure of our patent system shapes how innovative our drugs are.

In biomedicine we have a problem called target herding: most companies chase the same biological targets because they are de-risked, which means we explore far less of the biological space than we could. The cleanest way to see why is through risk. Two kinds matter in drug discovery. Target risk captures the biological uncertainty: is this protein causally involved in the disease, and will hitting it help a patient without unacceptable toxicity? Molecule design and optimization risk is the downstream problem, conditional on the target: designing a novel molecule against a target2 and improving potency, selectivity, safety and a myriad of other features of a chemical (e.g. small molecule) or biological (e.g. antibody). That is mostly in the realm of chemistry and is intrinsically far more tractable and predictable; given a validated target, good teams usually reach a decent molecule.

The patent system then further disincentivizes companies from taking target risk, because it rewards novel chemical matter, not novel biology. Composition of matter is what most patents protect. That refers to a specific molecule, which means that they don’t protect the insight that a target is worth drugging at all.

Target herding then follows almost mechanically from the above mentioned constraints: on one hand the fact that is genuinely harder to uncover more of these and then that the patent system does not reward it. Whoever validates a novel target (and implicitly, discovers new biology) bears the enormous target risk but can’t capture the reward due to the way the patent system is designed: once a first-in-class drug3 posts convincing clinical data, the target is validated, and that validation is essentially public. Competitors then design distinct molecules against the same de-risked target, and each fast-follower earns its own strong patent. So firms end up piling onto proven targets instead of validating new ones, so we get wave after wave of drugs aimed at the same type of biology.

A well-known non-profit leader who funds work on the molecular basis of deadly diseases, including AI-driven efforts to find novel targets, told me the current IP system makes it nearly impossible for the institution he supports to capture the value it creates by uncovering new biology. He's glad to keep funding it regardless, but believes everyone would be better served if that value were capturable, and that today's incentives are badly skewed.

The irony is that the AI-for-biology companies drawing the largest rounds are aimed mostly at the same well-served problem of molecule design and optimization. For example, Chai Discovery, now valued at $3.8 billion, enormous by early-stage biotech standards, and Isomorphic Labs are both, at heart, at molecule design and optimization engines: they design better compounds faster and with more accuracy, given a target. This is great, but as I and others have argued before, expanding the frontier of validated targets would be worth more overall to society. Yet this is precisely the part that the patent system does not incentivize. It turns out even AI-driven companies ultimately respond to economic and legal incentives!

The same principle applies, I suspect, well beyond medicine. Diffusion is hard, and the rate at which a technology actually spreads through an economy is not entirely or even mainly predicted by the raw pace of its underlying progress. A capability existing is not the same as a capability being absorbed into institutions, and, perhaps most important of all, translated into outcomes people care about.

And there is expansive evidence this is the case.

Walking around the world today one might notice that it is weirdly unchanged. LLMs can spawn agents and write complex applications, yet something as mundane as customer service still hasn’t been automated well. In fact, often it’s the automated chatbots that are the worst part of the experience. GDP is up, which is good, but it is not dramatically up. And entry-level jobs, despite repeated warnings of an apocalypse, seem largely intact, if not increasing.

To many, this is surprising. Just the other day I was at a conference where someone remarked that if he could have seen today’s AI capabilities a few years ago, he would have been astonished — and would have assumed the world by now would look far more transformed, with much higher GDP growth. It was offered as a fresh observation. But in fact, it has been made before, and this whole trajectory was quite predictable to those thinking about real world barriers to diffusion. I remember a Progress Conference in 2023 where the economist Tyler Cowen made exactly this argument to a room full of AGI-pilled attendees, many of whom were frankly incredulous. The capabilities, he suggested, would arrive faster than the changes they were meant to produce; GDP growth would disappoint relative to the hype, and there would be no massive job displacement. So far, the data seem to bear him out.

The people who saw this coming simply have a better feel for friction for how slowly and unevenly a technology actually diffuses into the world. Strangely, it seems to me that the core San Francisco tech scene, full of exceptionally intelligent people, does not. How can so many smart people share this one blind spot?

My view is that certain communities in San Francisco (which I shall henceforth call “SF people”, even though I do not mean literally everyone or even most people in SF) have become something close to a monoculture, and this monoculture has two reinforcing features. The first is that it has become genuinely low-status to suggest AGI might not be wholly transformative, at least not on its own. The people who were early and right about AI’s potential made a great deal of money, and being right about the big thing has hardened into an assumption that they are right about everything. To question the most extreme claims is to be marked as dim, low-IQ, insufficiently “AGI-pilled.” The belief persists that anyone who works at a lab, specially a CEO, holds secrets about the future that no outsider can access. The result is self-censorship: a lot of smart people I know in San Francisco see the bottlenecks to AI’s diffusion and say nothing to seem more “AGI-pilled”.

But how could such smart people be wrong… About anything? I do not think there is anything weird or unusual about that and in a wiser era we would find it easier to articulate. I have said before that the best human is very far from the average human, but God is much further way from the best human still. That is to say that nobody, no matter how smart, powerful and experienced, has all the answers.

Not only that, but I think the winners of the AI race might be miscalibrated in a way that might have helped in their core endeavour, developing AI, but maladaptive when it comes to judging things beyond that. Delusion is often adaptive in startups: an unreasonable conviction is exactly what lets a small group attempt the impossible and occasionally pull it off. Byrne Hobart and Tobias Huber make a version of this case in Boom, arguing that financial bubbles, usually maligned as destructive, have in fact been an engine of breakthrough progress: what looks like collective delusion is often what funds and forces genuine advance. But that cuts both ways. Being productively delusional and winning does not make one right about everything else. In fact, the very trait that produced the success also might inflate confidence in unproductive ways in other areas.

The second feature of this monoculture is a kind of counterfeit contrarianism. Because most of the outside world has long been skeptical of AI’s potential, people in San Francisco feel like brave dissenters. This is despite the fact that, within their own circles, holding those views is the safe and status-conferring position. Believing yourself a misunderstood contrarian is intoxicating, and it makes the underlying conviction harder to dislodge.

Back when I was an academic, I often noticed that academics were, on the whole, deeply progressive, yet thought of themselves as contrarians. This was at least in part because most had come from places more conservative than the university. They’d gather, compare themselves to the outside world rather than to each other, and conclude that their progressivism was somehow brave, despite it being the plain consensus of the room. In my view, SF has done the same thing with AI. In elite tech circles it is simply not contrarian to take AGI seriously; if anything the reverse. But because the comparison class is always someone else: for example, a policy person in DC, the feeling of embattled dissent survives contact with reality.

The question, I suppose, is whether any of this matters. Why would it be bad? For all I know, the AGI God frenzy should continue in the tech bubble. But it’s seeping into general public discourse in a way that might realign priorities in a way that is bad.

At the most basic level, I think being closer to the empirical truth is simply better than being further from it. But there is a more concrete cost: mistaken beliefs can lead to mistaken priorities. Given that I do expect AI to be disruptive (albeit not necessarily in the same ways the SF crowd thinks), this might be a particularly bad times to have bad priorities.

Again, I shall bring the example of medicine: we might be aiming or effort at the wrong bottlenecks. In medicine, as I’ve argued, regulatory reform gets a tiny fraction of the attention lavished on AI-enabled biology and even within AI-enabled biology, the interventions that would actually move the needle are the ones that often seem less funded.

And this goes well beyond medicine. We fixate on AGI gods, while more mundane problems pile up unattended. The social fabric is fraying in plain sight. More and more young adults cannot afford a house or sustain a relationship. People pour their youth into gambling apps, some of them now made more powerful by the very AI we keep discussing. People are de-skilling as they hand more thinking to machines. I sometimes say I worry less that AI will take my job than that people will grow too incurious to read at all. Every one of these problems needs people working on it. Being in the thrall of digital deities that will magically dissolve all our problems pulls attention away from the simpler, more human troubles that are already here.

1

Milan Cvitkovic pointed out that it is not clear that the regulatory reforms around faster in-human data spearheaded China’s rise. In 2015 China did a bunch of policy reforms that included expansion of coverage, clearing up some regulatory decision backlog and others and it is hard to say which ones were the most consequential. This article argues it was the coverage expansion. I explained in this X post why I doubt that article to some extent. Either way, I think everyone agrees that faster in-human data is a large component of China’s strength (whether caused by regulatory reforms or not) and also that the proximal cause of China’s rise in biotech was policy change. You can find my exchange with Milan here.

2

This is in practice a bit more complicated, as not all drugs are molecules. Some are cells or gene therapies. Nonetheless, even here, the broad principles hold. Improving a T cell therapy against a known target is inherently less risky.

3

First-in-class drugs are often not the drugs that “win” commercially, as followers usually manage to optimize the chemistry better and learn from deficiencies from the first-in-class. So it’s hard for someone who pioneers a new approach to capture value.

Given that I do expect AI to be disruptive (albeit not necessarily in the same ways the SF crowd thinks), this might be a particularly bad times to have bad priorities.Again, I shall bring the example of medicine: we might be aiming or effort at the wrong bottlenecks. In medicine, as I’ve argued, regulatory reform gets a tiny fraction of the attention lavished on AI-enabled biology and even within AI-enabled biology, the interventions that would actually move the needle are the ones that often seem less funded.And this goes well beyond medicine. We fixate on AGI gods, while more mundane problems pile up unattended. The social fabric is fraying in plain sight. More and more young adults cannot afford a house or sustain a relationship. People pour their youth into gambling apps, some of them now made more powerful by the very AI we keep discussing. People are de-skilling as they hand more thinking to machines. I sometimes say I worry less that AI will take my job than that people will grow too incurious to read at all. Every one of these problems needs people working on it. Being in the thrall of digital deities that will magically dissolve all our problems pulls attention away from the simpler, more human troubles that are already here.1Milan Cvitkovic pointed out that it is not clear that the regulatory reforms around faster in-human data spearheaded China’s rise. In 2015 China did a bunch of policy reforms that included expansion of coverage, clearing up some regulatory decision backlog and others and it is hard to say which ones were the most consequential. This article argues it was the coverage expansion. I explained in this X post why I doubt that article to some extent. Either way, I think everyone agrees that faster in-human data is a large component of China’s strength (whether caused by regulatory reforms or not) and also that the proximal cause of China’s rise in biotech was policy change. You can find my exchange with Milan here. 2This is in practice a bit more complicated, as not all drugs are molecules. Some are cells or gene therapies. Nonetheless, even here, the broad principles hold. Improving a T cell therapy against a known target is inherently less risky.3First-in-class drugs are often not the drugs that “win” commercially, as followers usually manage to optimize the chemistry better and learn from deficiencies from the first-in-class. So it’s hard for someone who pioneers a new approach to capture value.

Or one can listen to the scientists behind “baby KJ,” the infant saved by a bespoke gene-editing therapy: they have everything they need scientifically and still cannot easily repeat it for the next child, because manufacturing costs, driven in part by regulatory requirements, stand in the way.

blocks.html_en: When people in the AI sphere do engage with regulation and governance in medicine, it often seems to happen in a rather superficial way. I have seen many times that argument that because most drugs fail for lack of efficacy, regulation can’t explain much of the slow-down in medical progress compared to basic science that we have witnessed in the last decades: after all, approving more inefficacious drugs won’t help. This analysis sounds superficially true, but it’s not. As I keep saying, when people talk about the importance of regulation in slowing down biomedical progress, they rarely mean the approval decision at the end. It is about the entire process upstream: how easily human data can be collected, and then how easily, once collected, it can actually be used.

blocks.html_en: In biomedicine we have a problem called target herding: most companies chase the same biological targets because they are de-risked, which means we explore far less of the biological space than we could. The cleanest way to see why is through risk. Two kinds matter in drug discovery. Target risk captures the biological uncertainty: is this protein causally involved in the disease, and will hitting it help a patient without unacceptable toxicity? Molecule design and optimization risk is the downstream problem, conditional on the target: designing a novel molecule against a target2 and improving potency, selectivity, safety and a myriad of other features of a chemical (e.g. small molecule) or biological (e.g. antibody). That is mostly in the realm of chemistry and is intrinsically far more tractable and predictable; given a validated target, good teams usually reach a decent molecule.

blocks.html_en: Target herding then follows almost mechanically from the above mentioned constraints: on one hand the fact that is genuinely harder to uncover more of these and then that the patent system does not reward it. Whoever validates a novel target (and implicitly, discovers new biology) bears the enormous target risk but can’t capture the reward due to the way the patent system is designed: once a first-in-class drug3 posts convincing clinical data, the target is validated, and that validation is essentially public. Competitors then design distinct molecules against the same de-risked target, and each fast-follower earns its own strong patent. blocks.html_en: To many, this is surprising. Just the other day I was at a conference where someone remarked that if he could have seen today’s AI capabilities a few years ago, he would have been astonished — and would have assumed the world by now would look far more transformed, with much higher GDP growth. blocks.html_en: My view is that certain communities in San Francisco (which I shall henceforth call “SF people”, even though I do not mean literally everyone or even most people in SF) have become something close to a monoculture, and this monoculture has two reinforcing features. The first is that it has become genuinely low-status to suggest AGI might not be wholly transformative, at least not on its own. The people who were early and right about AI’s potential made a great deal of money, and being right about the big thing has hardened into an assumption that they are right about everything. To question the most extreme claims is to be marked as dim, low-IQ, insufficiently “AGI-pilled.” The belief persists that anyone who works at a lab, specially a CEO, holds secrets about the future that no outsider can access. The result is self-censorship: a lot of smart people I know in San Francisco see the bottlenecks to AI’s diffusion and say nothing to seem more “AGI-pilled”.

blocks.html_en: Not only that, but I think the winners of the AI race might be miscalibrated in a way that might have helped in their core endeavour, developing AI, but maladaptive when it comes to judging things beyond that. Delusion is often adaptive in startups: an unreasonable conviction is exactly what lets a small group attempt the impossible and occasionally pull it off. Byrne Hobart and Tobias Huber make a version of this case in Boom, arguing that financial bubbles, usually maligned as destructive, have in fact been an engine of breakthrough progress: what looks like collective delusion is often what funds and forces genuine advance. But that cuts both ways. Being productively delusional and winning does not make one right about everything else. In fact, the very trait that produced the success also might inflate confidence in unproductive ways in other areas.

blocks.html_en: The second feature of this monoculture is a kind of counterfeit contrarianism. Believing yourself a misunderstood contrarian is intoxicating, and it makes the underlying conviction harder to dislodge.

blocks.html_en: Back when I was an academic, I often noticed that academics were, on the whole, deeply progressive, yet thought of themselves as contrarians. This was at least in part because most had come from places more conservative than the university. They’d gather, compare themselves to the outside world rather than to each other, and conclude that their progressivism was somehow brave, despite it being the plain consensus of the room. In my view, SF has done the same thing with AI. In elite tech circles it is simply not contrarian to take AGI seriously; if anything the reverse. But because the comparison class is always someone else: for example, a policy person in DC, the feeling of embattled dissent survives contact with reality.

content_html_zh:
编辑：需要明确的是，我并不是说科幻科技界的每个人甚至大多数人都这么认为。 但有些人肯定会这样做（例如，开头的对话是逐字记录的），而这篇文章是关于一个特定的核心场景，其观点在话语和政策制定中具有不成比例的分量。

在最近的一次晚宴上，人工智能实验室的一个人非常直白地问我为什么要做我所做的事情——为什么我要写关于医学进步的监管瓶颈的文章，为什么我要把时间花在与临床试验相关的政策上。 他用一种最能概括为怜悯的眼神看着我。

我告诉他我的想法：在人工智能时代，医学将比以往任何时候都更加受到监管和临床试验的困扰，而投入到更快的临床前研究中的数十亿美元不会触及这个问题，尽管它本身并不吸引人。 我提到了住房：几十年来，我们拥有建造更好住房的技术，但它比以往任何时候都更昂贵，因为住房是一个政治意愿的问题，而不是纯粹的能力问题。

他难以置信地看着我。 当然，像我这样的聪明人应该知道人工智能，或者更好地说，AGI 很快就会具有超级说服力——在一系列基准测试中，它的说服力已经超过了专业辩手。 我说：“嗯。” 他说，“是的，是的”，语气就像一个深谙事物的人，像我这样的凡人，不是人工智能实验室的员工，根本无法掌握这些东西。 他再次用那种怜悯的感觉看着我，就像一个人看着一只稍微有精神障碍但可爱的动物等待即将被屠杀一样。

那天晚上，我彻夜难眠，翻来覆去，想知道我的生活是否还有意义。 我所做的每一个决定是否在某种程度上都是一个错误。 我可以做得更好吗？

但当太阳升起时，我又回到了同样的想法：无论人工智能变得多么“智能”，智能往往都不是现实世界中事物变化的主要瓶颈。 当比你聪明并且能够获取特权信息的人坚持相反的观点时，你就很难坚持这种信念。 毕竟，这一切可能只是等待被宰杀的天真的仓鼠的“应对”。

但是，我还是会坚持自己的信念。

因为这些实验室的人们通过押注曾经看似疯狂的想法而发了财，所以现在世界几乎相信他们所说的一切。 我认为这是一个错误。 人工智能并不能解决大多数人真正关心的问题，包括医学问题，除非我们清楚地思考这些问题。 目前，我不相信我们是这样的，或者至少没有达到我们能够做到的程度。 我的案例很简单，它来自两个方向。 一是我在旧金山的社会动态中观察到的，以及那里的人们如何谈论这一切。 另一个是我在一个我碰巧了解的领域注意到的：医学。

为了证明人工智能的风险合理性，最常被引用的承诺之一是它将“治愈疾病”。 每个主要人工智能实验室的首席执行官都这么说，而且投资者似乎也同意：任何拥有人工智能故事的生物技术初创公司都拥有令人印象深刻的估值，即使更传统的生物技术公司因融资而苦苦挣扎并死亡。 但正如我长期以来所主张的那样，整个事业受到许多与“智能”本身无关的事情的瓶颈，而这一点经常被忽视的程度令人奇怪。

如果你将科学进步视为智力的粗略代表，并询问它是否能够单独阻碍进步，那么证据无处不在。 以埃鲁姆定律为例：几十年来，每美元研发批准的新药数量一直在下降，尽管我们的科学工具已经变得更加强大，这与更多原始能力的存在所预测的完全相反。 或者以像 Adaptimmune 这样的公司为例，该公司已将两种治疗罕见癌症的变革性疗法推向市场，但由于开发这些疗法的成本高昂，该公司仍在为生存而奋斗。 或者我们可以听听“婴儿 KJ”（通过定制基因编辑疗法拯救的婴儿）背后的科学家们的心声：他们拥有科学上所需的一切，但仍然无法轻易地为下一个孩子重复这种治疗，因为部分由监管要求驱动的制造成本阻碍了这一过程。

具体来说，在生物制药领域，一个巨大的瓶颈是临床试验（我知道我一直在谈论这个），目前临床试验需要大约七年的时间，每种药物的成本超过 10 亿美元。 审判不仅仅是形式。 它们生成的数据正是能够训练更好模型的数据：人类数据，这最终是不可替代的。

我们有大量证据表明，更快的临床试验对于生物医学创新非常重要，无论是直接的还是间接的，通过二阶效应（例如提高该行业从业人员的风险偏好并通过快速反馈循环帮助更好地调整激励措施）。 其中包括从强有力的经济论文（显示在其他条件相同的情况下，更短的试验可以大幅增加对疾病领域的投资）到中国的自然实验。 中国有可能在生物技术领域领先于美国，中国生物技术公司包揽了西方大型制药许可交易的一半以上。 仅仅十年前，这个百分比为零。 这种转变发生时，中国在基础科学方面仍然较差，这主要是由于监管改革允许使用人类数据进行更快的迭代学习1。

试验本身可以变得更短、信息更丰富、效果更好，包括人工智能。 我特别看好的一个领域是替代终点和生物标志物，人工智能可以将药物是否发挥作用的离散、粗略的读数转变为快速、连续的读数。 这反过来又会极大地优化试验。 对于某些适应症，如果找到合适的替代品，试验的速度和成本可能会提高 10 倍之多。 这甚至没有考虑简单地优化试验而不一定缩短试验的好处：想象一下，有正确的生物标志物可以告诉您治疗是否足够早地发挥作用。

但即使在这里，约束约束也不完全是智力。 很多时候，这就是治理。 我一直在与试图精确构建这些生物标记物的公司交谈，他们一次又一次遇到的是访问基础数据是多么困难。 有些人已经等待了一年，等待美国国立卫生研究院发布他们可以用来产生更好的生物标志物的成像数据集。 如果需要与 FDA 互动才能验证其终点，那就更糟糕了：我之前曾写过如何将骨矿物质密度 (BMD) 用作骨质疏松症试验替代终点的验证花了 12 年（！），尽管支持它的数据已经完整存在，而且所做的分析基本上都是回归。

当人工智能领域的人们确实参与医学监管和治理时，它似乎常常以一种相当肤浅的方式发生。 我多次看到这样的论点，即由于大多数药物因缺乏疗效而失败，与过去几十年我们所目睹的基础科学相比，监管无法解释医学进步的大部分放缓：毕竟，批准更多无效的药物无济于事。 这种分析表面上听起来正确，但事实并非如此。 正如我一直说的，当人们谈论监管对于减缓生物医学进步的重要性时，他们很少指的是最后的批准决定。 它涉及上游的整个过程：收集人类数据有多容易，以及收集后实际使用起来有多容易。

我对临床试验了解最多，但这并不是治理和政策减缓进展的唯一领域。 另一个例子与我们的专利制度的结构如何影响我们药物的创新程度有关。

在生物医学中，我们遇到一个称为“目标羊群效应”的问题：大多数公司都追逐相同的生物目标，因为它们降低了风险，这意味着我们探索的生物空间远远少于我们所能探索的。 了解原因的最简单方法是通过风险。 在药物发现中，有两种因素很重要。 目标风险捕捉了生物学的不确定性：这种蛋白质是否与疾病有关？击中它是否会帮助患者而不会产生不可接受的毒性？ 分子设计和优化风险是下游问题，以目标为条件：针对目标2设计一种新分子，并提高化学物质（例如小分子）或生物物质（例如抗体）的效力、选择性、安全性和许多其他特征。 这主要是在化学领域，本质上更容易处理和预测。给定一个经过验证的目标，优秀的团队通常会达到一个不错的分子。

专利制度进一步抑制公司承担目标风险，因为它奖励的是新颖的化学物质，而不是新颖的生物学。 大多数专利保护的是物质的成分。 这指的是一个特定的分子，这意味着它们根本不能保护目标值得用药的洞察力。

然后，目标羊群效应几乎机械地遵循上述限制：一方面，事实是确实更难发现更多这些，然后专利制度不会奖励它。 无论是谁验证了一个新的靶点（隐含地，发现了新的生物学），都承担着巨大的靶点风险，但由于专利制度的设计方式而无法获得回报：一旦一流药物3发布了令人信服的临床数据，靶点就得到了验证，而且验证基本上是公开的。 然后，竞争对手针对相同的降低风险的目标设计不同的分子，每个快速追随者都获得了自己的强大专利。 因此，公司最终会堆积经过验证的目标，而不是验证新的目标，因此我们得到了一波又一波针对同一类型生物学的药物。

一位著名的非营利组织领导者资助致命疾病分子基础的研究工作，包括人工智能驱动的寻找新靶标的工作，他告诉我，当前的知识产权制度使得他支持的机构几乎不可能通过发现新的生物学来获取其创造的价值。 不管怎样，他很高兴继续为其提供资金，但他相信，如果能够获得这种价值，每个人都会得到更好的服务，而今天的激励措施严重扭曲。

具有讽刺意味的是，获得最大轮融资的生物人工智能公司主要针对分子设计和优化这一同样得到良好解决的问题。 例如，Chai Discovery 目前估值 38 亿美元，按照早期生物技术标准来看是巨大的，而 Isomorphic Labs 本质上都是分子设计和优化引擎：它们在给定目标的情况下更快、更准确地设计更好的化合物。 这很好，但正如我和其他人之前所说的那样，扩大经过验证的目标范围对于社会整体来说更有价值。 但这恰恰是专利制度不鼓励的部分。 事实证明，即使是人工智能驱动的公司最终也会对经济和法律激励做出反应！

我怀疑，同样的原则也适用于医学以外的领域。 扩散是困难的，一项技术在经济中实际传播的速度并不完全甚至主要是由其潜在进步的原始速度来预测的。 现有的能力与被吸收到机构中的能力不同，也许最重要的是，能力转化为人们关心的结果。

有大量证据表明情况确实如此。

今天走遍世界，人们可能会注意到它奇怪地没有改变。 法学硕士可以派生代理并编写复杂的应用程序，但像客户服务这样平凡的事情仍然没有很好地实现自动化。 事实上，自动聊天机器人通常是体验中最糟糕的部分。 GDP 增长了，这是好事，但增长并不显着。 尽管一再警告世界末日，入门级工作即使没有增加，也基本完好无损。

对许多人来说，这令人惊讶。 就在前几天，我参加了一个会议，有人说，如果他几年前就能看到今天的人工智能能力，他一定会感到惊讶，并且会认为现在的世界会发生更大的变化，GDP 增长率也会更高。 这是一个新鲜的观察结果。 但事实上，这种情况以前就已经发生过，对于那些思考现实世界传播障碍的人来说，整个轨迹是可以预测的。 我记得在 2023 年的一次进步会议上，经济学家泰勒·考恩 (Tyler Cowen) 在满屋子的 AGI 与会者面前准确地提出了这一论点，其中许多人坦率地表示怀疑。 他表示，这些能力将比它们原本要产生的变化更快地到来；相对于炒作而言，GDP 增长将令人失望，而且不会出现大规模就业岗位流失。 到目前为止，数据似乎证实了他的观点。

看到这一情况的人们只是对摩擦有更好的感受，因为技术实际上传播到世界上是多么缓慢和不均匀。 奇怪的是，在我看来，旧金山核心科技圈充满了异常聪明的人，但事实并非如此。 这么多聪明人怎么能分享这个盲点呢？

我的观点是，旧金山的某些社区（我以后将其称为“旧金山人”，尽管我并不是指旧金山的每个人，甚至不是旧金山的大多数人）已经变得接近单一文化，而这种单一文化有两个强化特征。 首先，认为通用人工智能可能不会带来彻底的变革，至少它本身不会带来彻底的变革，这已经变得非常低级了。 那些很早就对人工智能的潜力做出正确判断的人赚了很多钱，而对大事的正确判断已经变成了一种假设，即他们对所有事情都是正确的。 质疑最极端的说法就会被标记为昏暗、低智商、不够“通用人工智能”。 人们始终相信，任何在实验室工作的人，尤其是首席执行官，都掌握着外人无法得知的未来秘密。 结果就是自我审查：我在旧金山认识的很多聪明人都看到了人工智能传播的瓶颈，但他们什么也没说，看起来更“被 AGI 充斥”。

但这么聪明的人怎么会错呢…… 关于什么？ 我不认为这有什么奇怪或不寻常的，在一个更明智的时代，我们会发现它更容易表达。 我以前说过，最好的人与一般人相差甚远，但神与最好的人还差得很远。 也就是说，没有人，无论多么聪明、多么强大、多么有经验，都知道所有的答案。

不仅如此，我认为人工智能竞赛的获胜者可能会在某种程度上做出错误的校准，这可能有助于他们的核心努力，即开发人工智能，但在判断除此之外的事情时却适应不良。 妄想在初创公司中通常是适应性的：不合理的信念正是让一小群人尝试不可能的事情并偶尔成功的原因。 伯恩·霍巴特（Byrne Hobart）和托比亚斯·胡贝尔（Tobias Huber）在《繁荣》一书中提出了这一案例的一个版本，他们认为，通常被认为具有破坏性的金融泡沫实际上是突破性进步的引擎：看似集体错觉的东西往往会资助并推动真正的进步。 但这是双向的。 富有成效的妄想和胜利并不意味着一个人在其他一切事情上都是正确的。 事实上，带来成功的特质也可能会在其他领域以非生产性的方式增强信心。

这种单一文化的第二个特征是一种假冒的逆向主义。 由于外界大多数人长期以来一直对人工智能的潜力持怀疑态度，旧金山的人们感觉自己是勇敢的持不同政见者。 尽管事实是，在他们自己的圈子内，持有这些观点是安全的、有地位的立场。 相信自己是一个被误解的逆向投资者是令人陶醉的，而且它使潜在的信念更难以摆脱。

当我还是一名学者时，我经常注意到学者们总体上是非常进步的，但他们却认为自己是逆向者。 这至少部分是因为大多数人来自比大学更保守的地方。 他们聚集在一起，将自己与外部世界而不是彼此进行比较，并得出结论，他们的进步主义在某种程度上是勇敢的，尽管这是房间里的明显共识。 在我看来，SF在AI上也做了同样的事情。 在精英科技圈子里，认真对待 AGI 根本就不是逆向思维。如果有什么相反的话。 但由于比较阶层总是其他人：例如，华盛顿特区的政策制定者，因此与现实接触后，四面楚歌的异议感觉仍然存在。

我想，问题是这些是否重要。 为什么会不好呢？ 据我所知，AGI 上帝的狂热应该会在科技泡沫中继续下去。 但它正在渗透到公众的讨论中，可能会以一种不好的方式重新调整优先事项。

在最基本的层面上，我认为接近经验真理比远离经验真理要好。 但还有一个更具体的代价：错误的信念可能会导致错误的优先事项。 鉴于我确实预计人工智能会具有颠覆性（尽管不一定像科幻小说人群所认为的那样），这可能是一个特别糟糕的时期，不能优先考虑。

我将再次举医学的例子：我们的目标或努力可能是错误的瓶颈。 正如我所说，在医学领域，监管改革只占人工智能生物学的一小部分，即使在人工智能生物学领域，真正能起到推动作用的干预措施往往似乎资金较少。

这远远超出了医学的范畴。 我们专注于通用人工智能之神，而更多的平凡问题却无人理会。 社会结构正在明显地磨损。 越来越多的年轻人买不起房子或维持一段关系。 人们将青春倾注在赌博应用程序中，其中一些应用程序现在因我们不断讨论的人工智能而变得更加强大。 人们将更多的思考交给机器，从而降低了技能。 我有时会说，我不太担心人工智能会抢走我的工作，而是担心人们会变得缺乏好奇心而根本不再阅读。 这些问题中的每一个问题都需要人们来解决。 数字神灵会神奇地解决我们所有的问题，让我们将注意力从已经存在的更简单、更人性化的问题上转移开。
